title: Graphical Models and Hidden Markov Models
description: Bayesian networks, conditional independence and d-separation, exact inference, hidden Markov models and undirected models.
overview: A joint distribution over n binary variables has 2ⁿ − 1 free parameters, which is hopeless for n = 50. Real problems have structure: most variables depend directly on only a few others. A probabilistic graphical model uses a graph to record which variables depend on which, and in doing so factors the joint distribution into small, manageable pieces. The graph also tells us, by inspection, which variables are independent of which others, and organizes the computation of the probabilities we want.
This chapter covers directed models (Bayesian networks), the inference calculations on them, the most important sequence model (the hidden Markov model), and undirected models.
objectives: Write the factorization of a joint distribution from a Bayesian network and count its parameters.
Read conditional independence from a graph using d-separation, and explain explaining away.
Compute marginals and posteriors by variable elimination on small examples.
Run the forward and Viterbi algorithms of a hidden Markov model.
Describe Markov random fields and conditional random fields.

sections.title: Bayesian networks
body: Consider why grass is wet: it may have rained, or the sprinkler may have run, and the sprinkler is less likely to run if it rained. Draw an arrow from each cause to each effect: Rain → Sprinkler, Rain → Wet, Sprinkler → Wet. The picture records which things influence which directly, and the probabilities need only describe each variable given its direct causes, such as P(wet | rain, sprinkler). A **Bayesian network** is a directed acyclic graph with one node per random variable. Each node has a conditional distribution given its **parents** in the graph, and the joint distribution is the product:

body.eq: P(x₁, …, x_n) = Π_i P( x_i | parents(x_i) )

body: For discrete variables each factor is a **conditional probability table**. The saving is large: if each of 30 binary variables has at most 3 parents, the network needs at most 30 × 2³ = 240 numbers instead of 2³⁰ − 1 (over a billion).

example.title: A three-variable chain
example.problem: A → B → C, with P(A = 1) = 0.6, P(B = 1 | A = 1) = 0.9, P(B = 1 | A = 0) = 0.2, P(C = 1 | B = 1) = 0.7, P(C = 1 | B = 0) = 0.1. Find P(C = 1) and the number of parameters.
solution: Parameters: 1 for A, 2 for B (one per value of A), 2 for C: 5 instead of 2³ − 1 = 7. The saving grows quickly with the number of variables.

body: Familiar models are Bayesian networks. **Naive Bayes** has a class variable as the parent of every feature. A **hidden Markov model** is a chain of hidden states, each with one observation. A **mixture model** has a latent variable pointing to the observed variables. The graph makes the assumptions explicit.

With fully observed data, each conditional table is estimated independently by counting: P(x_i = a | parents = b) = count(a, b)/count(b), usually with Laplace smoothing (a Dirichlet prior). If some variables are latent, use EM (see Mixture Models and EM). Learning the structure itself is harder: score structures with BIC or the marginal likelihood and search over graphs, or use independence tests. Causal reading of the arrows needs extra assumptions (see Causal Inference in the Data Science book).

check.q: A Bayesian network over 20 binary variables, each with at most 2 parents, needs at most how many probabilities?
wrong: 2²⁰ − 1

sections.title: Conditional independence and d-separation
body: The graph's main message is which variables are independent given others. There are three building blocks for a path through a node.

body.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 440 150' role='img' aria-label='Three small graphs: chain, fork and collider' font-family='system-ui, sans-serif' font-size='12'><defs><marker id='arr' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='7' markerHeight='7' orient='auto'><path d='M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z' fill='currentColor'/></marker></defs><g fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.5'><circle cx='30' cy='50' r='14'/><circle cx='80' cy='50' r='14'/><circle cx='130' cy='50' r='14'/><path d='M44,50 L64,50 M94,50 L114,50' marker-end='url(#arr)'/><circle cx='200' cy='50' r='14'/><circle cx='250' cy='80' r='14'/><circle cx='300' cy='50' r='14'/><path d='M210,60 L240,74 M290,60 L260,74' marker-end='url(#arr)' transform='translate(0,0)'/><circle cx='350' cy='30' r='14'/><circle cx='400' cy='80' r='14'/><circle cx='350' cy='130' r='14'/></g><g fill='currentColor' text-anchor='middle'><text x='30' y='54'>A</text><text x='80' y='54'>B</text><text x='130' y='54'>C</text><text x='200' y='54'>A</text><text x='250' y='84'>B</text><text x='300' y='54'>C</text><text x='80' y='110'>chain: A → B → C</text><text x='250' y='125'>collider: A → B ← C</text></g></svg>
body.caption: A chain A → B → C and a collider A → B ← C. In the chain, B blocks the path when observed. In the collider, B blocks the path until it (or a descendant) is observed.

list: **Chain** A → B → C and **fork** A ← B → C: A and C are dependent, but become independent once B is observed (B 'blocks' the path). Example: smoking → tar in lungs → cancer; given tar, smoking carries no further information about cancer.
**Collider** A → B ← C: A and C are independent when B is not observed, but become **dependent** once B (or any descendant of B) is observed.

body: **d-separation** generalizes this: two sets of variables are conditionally independent given a set Z if every path between them is blocked by Z, where a path is blocked by a chain or fork node in Z, or by a collider that is not in Z and has no descendant in Z. The **Markov blanket** of a node (its parents, children and its children's other parents) makes it independent of all the rest.

example.title: Explaining away
example.problem: An alarm A rings if there is a burglary B or an earthquake E (A = B OR E). B and E are independent, each with probability 0.1. Find P(B | A) and P(B | A, E).
solution: P(A) = 1 − 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.19. Burglary implies the alarm, so P(B | A) = P(B)/P(A) = 0.1/0.19 = 0.526.
Now we learn there was also an earthquake. The alarm is already explained, so the burglary is no more probable than usual: P(B | A, E) = P(B) = 0.1.
B and E are independent a priori, but become dependent given the alarm: learning one lowers belief in the other. This 'explaining away' is the signature of a collider.

sections.title: Exact inference
body: Inference means computing a marginal or a conditional probability, such as P(disease | symptoms). The brute-force way sums the joint over all other variables, which costs exponentially many terms. **Variable elimination** instead pushes the sums inside the product of factors and removes one variable at a time. For the chain A → B → C, P(C) = Σ_B P(C | B) Σ_A P(B | A)P(A): each sum is a small table, as in the earlier example.

list: On a **tree** or chain, the **sum-product** algorithm (belief propagation) computes all the marginals at once by passing messages along the edges in two sweeps, in time linear in the number of nodes.

On a general graph, the cost of variable elimination depends on the **treewidth**, the size of the largest table created, which is the number of variables in the largest clique of the best triangulation. The junction tree algorithm packages this. For graphs with large treewidth, exact inference is NP-hard.

Then use **approximate** inference: sampling (MCMC, importance sampling), variational methods (see Bayesian Methods), or loopy belief propagation, which runs message passing on a graph with cycles and often works well in practice.

example.title: A posterior by Bayes' rule on the chain
example.problem: In the A → B → C chain above, C is observed to be 1. Find P(A = 1 | C = 1).

sections.title: Hidden Markov models
body: Imagine you work in a windowless room and want to know the weather outside, but all you see is whether each colleague arrives with an umbrella. The weather (the hidden state) changes from day to day with some persistence, and the umbrellas (the observations) depend on the weather. From the umbrella sightings alone you reason about the hidden weather sequence. That is an HMM. A **hidden Markov model** (HMM) describes a sequence in which an unobserved state s_t evolves as a Markov chain (the next state depends only on the current state), and each state emits an observation x_t. It is parameterized by

list: the initial distribution π_i = P(s₁ = i),
the **transition matrix** A_ij = P(s_{t+1} = j | s_t = i),
the **emission** probabilities B_i(x) = P(x_t = x | s_t = i).

body: The joint distribution is P(s, x) = π_{s₁} B_{s₁}(x₁) Π_{t≥2} A_{s_{t−1}s_t} B_{s_t}(x_t). HMMs were the standard model for speech recognition (states are phonemes, observations are acoustic features), part-of-speech tagging, gene finding and many other sequence tasks. There are three problems.
How likely is an observation sequence? Summing over all N^T state sequences is infeasible, but the **forward** variable α_t(i) = P(x₁, …, x_t, s_t = i) satisfies a recursion that costs O(TN²):

example.title: Forward algorithm for a weather HMM
example.problem: Two hidden states, Rain and Sun. π = (0.5, 0.5), transitions: stay with probability 0.7, switch with 0.3. Emissions: P(umbrella | Rain) = 0.9, P(umbrella | Sun) = 0.2. We see umbrella on two consecutive days. Find the probability of the observations and the probability that day 2 is rainy.
solution: P(observations) = 0.3105 + 0.0410 = 0.3515, and P(day 2 rainy | observations) = 0.3105/0.3515 = 0.883. This conditional is the filtering distribution.

body: What is the most likely hidden state sequence? Replace the sums by maxima: δ_{t+1}(j) = max_i [δ_t(i) A_ij] B_j(x_{t+1}), remember which i achieved the maximum, and trace back from the best final state.

example.title: Viterbi on the same data
example.problem: Find the most likely state sequence for the two umbrella days.
example.solution: δ₁ = (0.45, 0.10). δ₂(Rain) = max(0.45 · 0.7, 0.10 · 0.3) · 0.9 = 0.315 · 0.9 = 0.2835, reached from Rain. δ₂(Sun) = max(0.45 · 0.3, 0.10 · 0.7) · 0.2 = 0.135 · 0.2 = 0.027, also from Rain. The best final state is Rain (0.2835), so the path is Rain, Rain.

body: Given only observations, estimate π, A and B by EM, called the **Baum–Welch** algorithm. The E-step uses the forward and a backward recursion to compute the posterior probability of each state, and of each pair of consecutive states, at every time. The M-step re-estimates each parameter from these expected counts: A_ij is the expected number of transitions i → j divided by the expected number of visits to i.

body.note: HMMs have been largely replaced in speech and language by recurrent networks and transformers, which model long-range structure better, but state-space models (Kalman filters for continuous states, HMMs for discrete) remain central in tracking, control, bioinformatics and time-series analysis.

sections.title: Undirected models: MRFs and CRFs
terms: partition function of a graphical model
body: When the relations between variables are symmetric and have no natural direction (neighboring pixels, interacting atoms, friends in a network), an undirected graph is more natural. A **Markov random field** (MRF) defines the joint distribution through non-negative **potential functions** ψ_c on the cliques c of the graph:

body.eq: P(x) = (1/Z) Π_c ψ_c(x_c),    Z = Σ_x Π_c ψ_c(x_c)

body: The **partition function** Z makes the distribution sum to one. Computing it is generally intractable, because it sums over all configurations, and this is the main difficulty of learning MRFs. Conditional independence is simpler than in directed models: a variable is independent of all others given its neighbors.

list: The **Ising model** has binary spins x_i ∈ {−1, +1} and pairwise potentials ψ(x_i, x_j) = exp(J x_i x_j). With J > 0 it favors neighbors that agree, as in image denoising, where the observed pixels are tied to hidden clean pixels that prefer to equal their neighbors.
A **Boltzmann machine** is a fully connected MRF over binary units with hidden units; the restricted version (bipartite) was an early deep learning building block.

A **conditional random field** (CRF) models P(y | x) directly, with potentials that may depend on the whole input x, so there is no need to model the inputs themselves. Linear-chain CRFs were standard for tagging sequences, such as names in text, and are often attached on top of a neural network's outputs.

example.title: A partition function
example.problem: Two binary variables x₁, x₂ ∈ {0, 1} share the potential ψ(x₁, x₂) = 3 if x₁ = x₂ and 1 otherwise. Find Z and P(x₁ = x₂).
example.solution: The four configurations have values 3, 1, 1, 3, so Z = 8. P(x₁ = x₂) = (3 + 3)/8 = 0.75.

quiz.q: Six binary variables form a chain X₁ → X₂ → … → X₆. How many free parameters does the Bayesian network need?
quiz.why: The root needs 1 number and each of the 5 other variables needs 2 (one per value of its parent), so 1 + 5 × 2 = 11. The value 63 = 2⁶ − 1 is the full joint table.

quiz.q: A network has edges A → C, B → C and C → D. Which factorization of the joint distribution does it encode?
quiz.a: P(A) P(B) P(C | A, B) P(D | C)
wrong: P(A) P(B | A) P(C | A, B) P(D | C)
P(A) P(B) P(C) P(D | C)
P(A | C) P(B | C) P(C) P(D | C)
quiz.why: Each variable contributes one factor conditioned on its parents. A and B have no parents, so their factors are unconditional, and C has parents A and B.

quiz.q: All variables are binary. In the data, x has parent b = 1 in 10 examples, and x = 1 in 3 of them. With Laplace smoothing (add 1 to each count), the estimate of P(x = 1 | b = 1) is
quiz.why: Smoothing adds 1 to the count of each value of x, so the numerator is 3 + 1 and the denominator is 10 + 2. This corresponds to a uniform Dirichlet prior.

quiz.q: In the network A → B ← C, B → D, the variable D is observed and B is not. What is the relationship between A and C?
quiz.a: They are dependent, since D is a descendant of the collider B
wrong: They are independent, since the collider B itself is not observed, so the path stays blocked
They are independent, since D blocks the path
They are dependent only if B itself is observed
quiz.why: A collider, or any descendant of it, that is observed opens the path. Because D is observed, the path A → B ← C is no longer blocked.

quiz.q: Ice cream sales and drownings are both caused by temperature (Ice cream ← Temperature → Drownings). Which statement is correct?
quiz.a: They are dependent if temperature is unobserved, and independent given the temperature
wrong: They are independent always, since neither causes the other
They are independent if temperature is unobserved, and dependent given the temperature
They are dependent always, since the common cause cannot be blocked
quiz.why: A fork node passes dependence when it is unobserved and blocks the path once it is observed.

quiz.q: A network has edges A → B, C → B, B → D and E → D. What is the Markov blanket of B?
wrong: {A, C, D}
{A, D}
{A, C, D, E, and every descendant of D}
quiz.why: The blanket is the parents (A, C), the children (D) and the children's other parents (E). Given these, B is independent of all other variables.

quiz.q: An alarm rings (A = B OR E) if there is a burglary B or an earthquake E, which are independent with P(B) = P(E) = 0.2. What is P(B | A)?
quiz.why: P(A) = 1 − 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.36, and a burglary always triggers the alarm, so P(B | A) = 0.2/0.36. Learning that the alarm rang raises belief in a burglary from 0.2.

quiz.q: Why is variable elimination cheaper than summing the full joint distribution over all other variables?
quiz.a: It pushes each sum inside the product, so only small tables over a few variables are created
wrong: It ignores configurations whose probability is small, summing only over the few most likely assignments of the other variables
It estimates the sums by sampling a few configurations
It removes the variables that are not parents of the query
quiz.why: Moving a sum past the factors that do not involve its variable lets one variable be eliminated at a time. The result is still exact. The cost then depends on the size of the largest table, i.e. the treewidth.

quiz.q: Use the chain A → B → C with P(A = 1) = 0.5, P(B = 1 | A = 1) = 0.8, P(B = 1 | A = 0) = 0.3, P(C = 1 | B = 1) = 0.9 and P(C = 1 | B = 0) = 0.2. If C = 1 is observed, what is P(A = 1 | C = 1)?
What happens when loopy belief propagation is run on a graph with cycles?
quiz.a: It is an approximation that often works well in practice, but it has no exactness guarantee
wrong: It is exact, as on trees, but needs many repeated sweeps around the cycles instead of the two used on a tree
It always fails to converge, so it is never used
It reduces to variable elimination with a smaller treewidth
quiz.why: Message passing is exact only on trees. On graphs with cycles the messages can be iterated anyway, which gives approximate marginals.

quiz.q: A two-state HMM has π = (0.6, 0.4), transition matrix [[0.9, 0.1], [0.2, 0.8]], and the same symbol x is seen on two days, with P(x | state 1) = 0.5 and P(x | state 2) = 0.1. What is the probability of the observations?
For the same HMM and data, what is the Viterbi value δ₂(state 2)?
wrong: 0.0062, the sum over both previous states
0.003, coming from state 1 on day 1
0.032, coming from state 2 on day 1
quiz.why: With δ₁ = (0.30, 0.04), the candidates are 0.30 · 0.1 = 0.03 and 0.04 · 0.8 = 0.032, so the best predecessor is state 2. Multiplying by the emission 0.1 gives 0.0032. The sum 0.0062 would be the forward value.

quiz.q: In the forward algorithm, α_t(i) is
quiz.a: the probability of the first t observations and of being in state i at time t
wrong: the probability of being in state i at time t, given all the observations, including the later ones
the probability of the t-th observation given state i
the probability of the best state sequence ending in state i
quiz.why: α_t(i) = P(x₁, …, x_t, s_t = i) is a joint probability, which is why summing it over i gives the likelihood. The best-path quantity is Viterbi's δ, and the posterior needs a backward pass too.

quiz.q: In Baum–Welch, the E-step gives expected counts: 1→1: 9, 1→2: 3, 2→1: 2, 2→2: 6. What does the M-step estimate for the transition probability A₁₂?
quiz.why: A₁₂ is the expected number of transitions 1 → 2 divided by the expected number of visits to state 1 as a source, 9 + 3 = 12. Dividing by 9 normalizes over transitions into state 2, which is the wrong direction.

quiz.q: Two binary variables share a potential ψ(x₁, x₂) = 4 when x₁ = x₂ = 1 and ψ = 1 for the other three configurations. What is P(x₁ = 1, x₂ = 1)?
quiz.why: The partition function is Z = 4 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 7, and the probability of a configuration is its potential divided by Z. Using 4 as a numerator without the sum of all four potentials gives probabilities that do not total one.

quiz.q: An Ising model has spins x_i ∈ {−1, +1} and pairwise potential ψ(x_i, x_j) = exp(J x_i x_j) with J = 0.5. How many times larger is the potential for two agreeing neighbors than for two disagreeing ones?
quiz.why: Agreeing neighbors give exp(+0.5) and disagreeing ones give exp(−0.5), so the ratio is exp(1) = e. The value 0.37 is the inverse ratio.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of a conditional random field over a Markov random field over (x, y) for tagging sequences?
quiz.a: It models P(y | x) directly, so inputs need not be modeled and potentials can depend on all of x
wrong: It has no partition function at all, so training reduces to counting, as for a Bayesian network
It is a directed model, so d-separation applies
It requires the cliques to be restricted to single nodes
quiz.why: A CRF still has a normalizing term, but it is computed per input x. By conditioning on x, it avoids modeling the complicated distribution of the inputs.

summary: A Bayesian network is a DAG with P(x) = Π P(x_i | parents(x_i)). The factorization cuts the parameter count from exponential to the sum of the local tables.
d-separation reads conditional independence off the graph. Observing a chain or fork node blocks the path; observing a collider (or its descendant) opens it, which causes explaining away.
Variable elimination and belief propagation compute marginals exactly; the cost depends on the treewidth. Otherwise use sampling, variational methods or loopy belief propagation.
An HMM has a hidden Markov chain and per-state emissions. The forward algorithm computes the likelihood in O(TN²), Viterbi decodes the best path, and Baum–Welch (EM) learns the parameters.
Markov random fields use clique potentials and a partition function; CRFs model P(y | x) discriminatively.

problems.q: For the chain A → B → C of the text, find P(B = 1 | C = 1).
In the burglary–earthquake–alarm model (A = B OR E, with P(B) = P(E) = 0.1), find P(B | A) and P(B | A, ¬E).
problems.solution: P(B | A) = 0.526 as computed. If we know there was no earthquake, the alarm must be due to the burglary: P(B | A, ¬E) = 1.

problems.q: In the weather HMM, the third day also shows umbrella. Compute α₃ and the probability of all three observations.
Count the free parameters in an HMM with N = 3 states and 5 possible observation symbols.
problems.solution: Initial distribution: N − 1 = 2. Transition matrix: N rows each with N − 1 free entries = 6. Emissions: N rows each with 4 free entries = 12. Total 20.

problems.q: An Ising model on 3 binary variables in a chain x₁ − x₂ − x₃ has pairwise potential ψ = 2 when neighbors agree and 1 otherwise. Compute Z.
problems.solution: Sum over the 8 configurations of ψ(x₁, x₂)ψ(x₂, x₃). Both pairs agree in 2 configurations (000, 111): 4 each → 8. Exactly one pair agrees in 4 configurations: 2 each → 8. No pairs agree in 2 configurations (010, 101): 1 each → 2. Z = 8 + 8 + 2 = 18.
